While he’s no longer the CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, Buffett’s legacy lives on with the decades spent guiding the conglomerate and being one of the most well-known and respected voices in finance.
To celebrate Buffett’s birthday and investing legacy, here’s a look back at a highlight for each decade of the “Oracle of Omaha’s” life.
Buffett was born Aug. 30, 1930. His father Howard was a former stockbroker. This would have a huge influence on Buffett’s decision to get involved in the business.
Buffett purchased his first stock at the age of 11. The purchase was for three shares of

, a natural gas company. Buffett bought the shares at $38 only to see them soon drop to $27 each. He waited until they hit $40 to sell for a profit. Shares later reached $200 each, a level that Buffett has since cited as a lesson in patience in investing.

Despite his growing wealth, Buffett has lived in the same house in Omaha, Nebraska since 1958. The home was purchased for $31,500. Adjusted for inflation, that would be the equivalent of over $355,805 today.

By the year 1965, Buffett had assumed control of textiles company Berkshire Hathaway, thanks to acquiring 49%. He became a director of the company and worked on gaining full control and also diversifying the company away from textiles.

Buffett became the author of the annual Berkshire Hathaway letters in the 1970s. These letters are considered must-reads for investors and every year, what Buffett writes to shareholders is analyzed with great detail. The letters include explanations for investments or why assets were sold. The letters also include life lessons and memorable quotes from the "Oracle of Omaha."
In 1988, Buffett started accumulating shares of

(NYSE:KO) for Berkshire Hathaway. After several large purchases, Berkshire Hathaway owned 7% of the company, worth $1.02 billion. Buffett has a long history with Coca-Cola, once selling bottles for a penny profit. Berkshire Hathaway still owns 400 million shares of KO, worth around $35.9 billion.

Buffett had been an investor in Geico shares dating back to 1951.
Buffett’s mentor and professor, was once the chairman of Geico. The insurance company is forever linked to two of the most well-known investors.

The 2000s represented a great period of fortune and giving for Buffett. In 2008, he became the richest man in the world, with Forbes valuing his wealth at $62 billion. Buffett took over the top spot from
, who had held the number one position for thirteen consecutive years. Buffett pledged in 2006 to give away the majority of his wealth after his death.
Berkshire Hathaway started buying stock in
(NASDAQ:AAPL) in 2016. Buffett has since admitted he wishes he would have bought shares earlier.

"It’s probably the best business I know in the world," Buffett told CNBC. Berkshire bought shares of Apple again throughout the decade to make it one of the biggest pieces of its investment portfolio.
"I don’t think of Apple as a stock. I think of it as a third business," Buffett told CNBC, referring to Apple being the company’s third-biggest holding behind Geico and railroad interests.
While Berkshire Hathaway has sold some of its Apple stock in recent years, the stock remains the largest holding the stock portfolio of the company with 227.9 million shares valued at $72.9 billion.
Buffett imparted an investor lesson when he sold his stake in the big four airlines. A longtime vocal non-supporter of buying airline stocks, he sold his stake worth around $7 billion at a loss.
